statement_en: Is there an absolute constant $C>0$ such that every integer $n$ with $\sigma(n)>Cn$ is the distinct sum of proper divisors of $n$?

issues: Restricting 'integer n' to natural numbers is harmless: σ is only meaningful for positive n, and n=0 is vacuous since σ(0)=0 in Mathlib.
'Distinct sum of proper divisors of n' is correctly read as 'n equals a sum of distinct proper divisors of n', i.e. n is semiperfect.
Small constants (C<1) fail at n=1, whose only proper-divisor subset is empty, but this only rules out some C; it does not distort the existential claim.
faithfulness.verdict: B is exactly A's YES assertion: there is a uniform constant C>0 such that every n with σ(n)>Cn is semiperfect, so a proof of B would settle the pos direction of A.
faithfulness.backtranslation: There exists a positive real constant $C$ such that every natural number $n$ with $\sigma(n) > C\,n$ is semiperfect. Here $\sigma(n)$ is the sum of all positive divisors of $n$. Semiperfect means there is a set $s$ of distinct proper divisors of $n$ (positive divisors other than $n$ itself) whose sum is exactly $n$. The same constant $C$ must work for every such $n$.
